meta.title: Who really said "Things don't turn up in this world until somebody turns them up"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Garfield's: this line appears verbatim in an 1881 biography crediting him. But the popular "1874 House speech" source is doubtful and unverifiable.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Things don't turn up in this world until somebody turns them up'?
meta.ogDescription: A real Garfield aphorism, documented in an 1881 biography — but the exact speech behind it can't be verified. Here's what the record actually shows.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine, period-documented Garfield line: it appears word-for-word in Emma Elizabeth Brown’s The Life and Public Services of James A. Garfield (1881), among a set of “Notable Extracts from His Speeches and Letters,” and it fits his terse, self-reliant style. But the exact origin is not verifiable — Brown groups it with unrelated aphorisms under a single “June 1874” heading, so the specific speech or letter behind it can’t be confirmed.

source.heading: The earliest documented source

source.excerpt: … the blast of a bugle can never make soldiers or win victories. ∗ Things don’t turn up in this world until somebody turns them up. ∗ We cannot study nature profoundly without bringing ourselves into communion with the spirit of art which pervades and fills the universe.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Sourced section, citing Brown’s 1881 biography, p. 437.
The exact wording is confirmed verbatim in the full 1881 text, printed among “Notable Extracts from His Speeches and Letters.”
Popular quote sites such as QuoteFancy reproduce it with no source at all — the usual pattern for a “magnet” name like Garfield.
source.excerptNote: In Brown’s 1881 biography the line is one of a run of asterisk-divided extracts sharing a single speech heading. Because the neighbouring lines leap from soldiery to art to grief, the “June 1874 House speech” label almost certainly can’t apply to all of them — which is why the exact source of this particular sentence stays open.
source.rightsNote: The source that documents this line — E. E. Brown’s biography — was first published in 1881, placing it firmly in the public domain in the United States. Garfield himself died in 1881, so anything he actually wrote or spoke is long out of copyright as well.

author.name: James A. Garfield
author.heading: About James A. Garfield
author.metaLine: 1831–1881 · 20th U.S. President, Union general & Ohio congressman
author.bio: James Abram Garfield (1831–1881) rose from an impoverished Ohio childhood to become a college president, Union major-general, nine-term congressman, and, in 1881, the 20th President of the United States. A noted orator with a taste for pithy, self-reliant maxims, he served only about six months before being shot in July 1881 and dying that September. His many aphorisms on effort and character were gathered into memorial biographies almost immediately after his death.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The sentence is a compact statement of the self-made ethic Garfield embodied — nothing in the world ‘turns up’ on its own; someone has to make it happen. It reads as a rebuke to the passive optimism of Dickens’s Mr. Micawber, forever ‘waiting for something to turn up.’

That message, plus Garfield’s log-cabin-to-White-House story, is exactly why the line travels well on motivational sites. The catch is that almost none of them say where he said it — and the one early source that does document it groups it too loosely to trust on the specific speech.
detailsBody: Brown’s 1881 compilation places this line under the heading ‘From a Speech in the House of Representatives, June, 1874.’ But the extracts sharing that heading range across church-and-state taxation, military bugle-calls, the ‘spirit of art,’ the solace of sorrow, and bravery — subjects no single House floor speech would plausibly cover.

The most honest reading is that the heading marks only the first extract, and the aphorisms after it are undated fragments Brown collected from various sources. So the wording is real and the author is Garfield, but the specific 1874-speech provenance repeated online is not something the record actually supports.
context.pull: Nothing turns up by itself — somebody has to turn it up.
